approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record

This bill would make the rules in the Offshore Electricity Infrastructure Amendment (Overlapping Applications) Regulations 2024 apply to all feasibility licence applications received before those regulations started.

The bill would require the Commonwealth to ensure a certain amount of clean dispatchable energy capacity is available by the end of 2030, and the minister must respond to advice from the Climate Change Authority about risks to meeting that goal.
Any change to the Industry Research and Development (Capacity Investment Scheme Program) would need Parliament's approval before taking effect.
Extend the regulatory parameters of the 2024 regulations to earlier feasibility licence applications.
Impose a 2030 deadline for a specified gigawatts of clean dispatchable energy capacity.
Require the minister to respond to Climate Change Authority advice on capacity risks.
Require parliamentary approval for amendments or revocation of the Capacity Investment Scheme program.
Applicants for feasibility licences under the offshore electricity infrastructure scheme, the Commonwealth government, and the Climate Change Authority.

Declared that the Customs Amendment (Expedited Seizure and Disposal of Engineered Stone) Bill 2024 and Electricity Infrastructure Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 would stand referred to the Federation Chamber after the second-reading debate.

Moved and seconded a motion to return the Electricity Infrastructure Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 from the Federation Chamber to the House, arguing that its retrospective changes to offshore wind licensing required parliamentary scrutiny; the question was deferred and debate adjourned.
Reported that the Electricity Infrastructure Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 had been returned to the House for further consideration and would be set down later that day.

Argued against the Electricity Infrastructure Legislation Amendment Bill 2025, saying Tasmania is already 100 per cent renewable and offshore wind could affect coastlines, shipping lanes and communities. Supported advancing the Marinus Link and called for public consultation and due process, while the minister said the bill would ensure fair treatment of feasibility licence applications and support offshore renewable energy projects.

Opposed retrospective amendments to offshore electricity legislation, arguing that the bill was rushed without industry consultation and should be referred to committee for proper scrutiny before proceeding.

Introduced the Electricity Infrastructure Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 to apply amended offshore renewable licensing rules consistently to earlier applications, saying this would improve administration and regulatory certainty; debate disputed its effects on energy prices, jobs, renewables and industry.

Argued that offshore wind projects risk losing social licence because of organised disinformation, and called for scrutiny of alleged foreign-linked campaigns and astroturfing targeting consultation and democratic institutions.
